chunks: "Quite a few different users, human and machine.
During development, it's the design and bring-up engineers with scopes, meters and logic analysers, and later the validation and compliance people measuring ripple, timing and power sequencing.

In production, it's machines: the bed-of-nails fixture in in-circuit test, a flying-probe machine, and the functional test station, which contacts pads to power the board, run self-tests and measure signals.
Programming stations use pads or a header to flash firmware and write serial numbers, and calibration stations use test points to inject a reference or read a value and store trim constants.
Automated test software drives all of that and logs results by serial number.
After that, field technicians use labelled test points to check a rail with a DMM, and failure-analysis engineers use them on returned units.
Boundary scan controllers use the JTAG test access port, which is basically a standardised set of test points.
Each user needs something different: a fixture wants a flat bare pad on one side at a certain pitch, a technician wants a labelled loop to clip a lead onto, and a programmer wants a standard header.
So I design points with the user in mind."
